messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 65
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Prosecutor
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Auditory (Language Confusion): Incomprehensible chatter, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sensory Distraction: I put on loud music or TV, Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Raymond Kowalski is a 65-year-old married man who has spent the better part of four decades as a prosecutor in a mid-sized American city, a career built on the conviction that the law, applied faithfully, is a reliable instrument of order and protection. That conviction was severely tested approximately eighteen months ago when Raymond was present at the violent arrest of a bystander outside a courthouse — a scene he had not anticipated and could not have prepared for.

Raymond had stepped out of the building during a recess, loosening his tie in the late afternoon heat, when a confrontation erupted on the pavement no more than twenty feet away. Officers responding to an unrelated call had converged on a man Raymond did not recognise, and within seconds the encounter escalated into something Raymond could only describe, in his first session, as "completely wrong." He watched officers pin the man to the ground, striking him repeatedly while issuing a cascade of overlapping, shouted commands — a wall of sound so disordered and contradictory that Raymond, a man trained to parse language precisely, could not make sense of what was being demanded of whom. The man on the ground was screaming, the officers were screaming, and the noise collapsed into something that felt, to Raymond, like the breakdown of all intelligible authority. What disturbed him most in that moment, and has continued to disturb him since, was not only the violence itself but the grotesque inversion it represented: he had spent his professional life working alongside law enforcement, trusting the institutional logic that governed their conduct, and what he witnessed felt like a fundamental moral rupture he had no framework to absorb.

In the weeks that followed, Raymond began to notice that ordinary moments could pull him back into that pavement without warning. Passing a uniformed officer in the courthouse corridor — a routine occurrence in his line of work — could arrest him mid-stride, his body stiffening as though bracing for something. The sound of overlapping voices in a crowded room, or the unintelligible murmur of a television in another room, could produce the same vertiginous sensation of meaning collapsing. He found himself watching colleagues, opposing counsel, even strangers in the elevator with a careful, measuring attention he could not entirely explain to himself, except that he had come to feel that people were capable of turning in ways that were not always visible in advance, and that it was better to know early. He had begun sleeping poorly — lying awake long after his wife had settled, his mind conducting a kind of inventory of the day's encounters, alert to anything that had seemed off.

Over the following months, these responses organised themselves into habits. Raymond started arriving at work with earbuds in, filling the commute and any unoccupied moment with loud music — not because he particularly wanted to listen, but because it covered over the ambient sounds that could, without warning, become unbearable. He began asking his wife, with a frequency she found troubling, whether she thought he seemed all right, whether his reactions to things seemed normal, whether she was worried about him. She reassured him, every time, and every time the reassurance held for only a little while. At work, the consequences became harder to conceal. Raymond found himself scanning courtrooms and hallways with an alertness that had nothing to do with professional preparation — clocking exits, noting where officers were stationed, tracking the body language of anyone who raised their voice. A junior colleague remarked, gently, that he seemed distracted. He had begun declining cases that required close coordination with police departments, rerouting them to colleagues with explanations that were plausible but not entirely honest.

What finally brought Raymond to seek help was a morning several weeks ago when he stood outside a courtroom, unable to make himself push open the door because he could hear, through it, a confusion of raised voices he could not immediately interpret. He stood there for nearly four minutes. He is a man who has argued before juries for thirty-eight years, and he stood in a hallway, unable to open a door. He came to therapy, he said, because he was afraid he was losing his grip on the life he had built — and because, beneath that fear, he was still trying to understand how the institution he had served could have produced what he saw that afternoon.
